assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are the working core of modern monetary policy analysis. Staggered contracts and the Calvo pricing device are standard building blocks. The Taylor rule shaped central-bank practice, and Woodford's work gave the framework its welfare-based foundations. Impact on both theory and policy practice is very large.
assessment.attribution: The credited group is large. The most separable contributions are Calvo's time-dependent pricing, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's synthesis and optimal-policy analysis. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and others made major further contributions. Choosing three entails a real attribution judgment, and the committee could reasonably draw the line differently.
assessment.maturity: The core contributions date from the 1970s to the early 2000s. They have been tested over decades, including the 2008 crisis, the post-pandemic inflation and policy debates. The field is mature, and no recent revision undermines its foundations.
uncertainties: Which three of the many contributors best capture the discovery.
Continuing debate about how well the framework fared after 2008 and in the recent inflation episode.
Possible overlap with other macro recognition, and a committee preference for other macro topics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The law and finance programme established that legal institutions, investor protection and ownership structure systematically shape financial development and corporate governance. It created a large cross-country empirical literature linking institutions to finance and growth. Its breadth and influence on research and policy are substantial.
assessment.attribution: The La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny collaboration is tightly integrated. A three-name selection leaves out Vishny, who co-authored the foundational papers, so attribution is a genuine difficulty. Shleifer's wider contributions in corporate finance and behavioural finance strengthen his claim but complicate how the prize would be framed.
assessment.maturity: The seminal papers date from 1997–2008, so decades of replication, extension and critique exist. The legal-origins hypothesis itself is contested, but the broader law-and-finance agenda has been consistently productive.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of legal-origins identification and of the coding of legal indices.
Exclusion of Vishny under the three-laureate limit.
Whether the committee would credit the framework or the contested empirical conclusions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work changed how economists understand technology, trade exposure and labour demand. It combines the task-based view of technological change, the skill-premium and race-between-education tradition, and credible local-labour-market evidence on import competition. It has had large influence on research and on public debate over inequality and trade adjustment.
assessment.attribution: The credits are distributed. Autor links both the task and trade-shock strands. Hanson is central to the China-shock evidence. Katz is central to the skill-premium and education-technology literature. Dorn is a key co-author of the China-shock papers, and task-framework co-authors outside this list also contributed. A three-name choice is defensible but incomplete.
assessment.maturity: The key papers span the 1990s to the 2010s. The China-shock results have been replicated and refined, and the task framework is widely adopted. Interpretation of long-run effects is still evolving, particularly with AI.
uncertainties: Debate over the magnitude and persistence of trade-shock effects.
Exclusion of Dorn and of co-authors outside the list.
Whether the prize would fit better with a different grouping of the technology and trade strands.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Methods for estimating demand with differentiated products, together with dynamic models of industries, underpin modern empirical industrial organisation. They are used in merger review, antitrust and many applied fields. The contribution is a methodological advance with broad downstream use.
assessment.attribution: The BLP demand framework is clearly attributable to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Pakes's dynamic-game work with Ericson, McGuire and Benkard adds to his claim. Bresnahan, Reiss and others have strong claims in the broader structural IO tradition and fall outside this selection.
assessment.maturity: BLP (1995) is thoroughly validated by three decades of widespread use and extensive methodological follow-up. The field is mature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to recognise the broader structural IO tradition instead of the BLP trio.
Exclusion of Bresnahan and others from a three-name set.
Weighing a methods-toolkit prize against substantive discoveries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Persson, Tabellini and Besley built the formal modern framework for studying how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes. Their work combines theory with empirical tests. It is a systematic research programme in political economics.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the clearest pair, with the integrated programme of the 'Political Economics' book and their constitutional-design papers. Besley's state-capacity and accountability contributions are distinct and substantial, and the three-name set fits the limit. Other contributors to political economics exist beyond this list.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s to the 2010s and has long been influential in research and policy. It has had extensive replication and extension, and the field is well established.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the political-economy theme recognised in recent prizes on institutions.
Whether the committee sees this as one discovery or several separate ones.
Mixed empirical robustness of some constitutional-effects results.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The firm-heterogeneity framework shifted trade theory from industries and countries to firms, explaining selection, exporter premia and new channels for gains from trade. It has had large influence on empirical and theoretical trade research and on policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the clear core. Helpman's contributions through monopolistic-competition trade models and firm-heterogeneity extensions (Helpman–Melitz–Yeaple) make a strong second name. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, among others, made important parallel contributions and sit outside this ballot's credited set. Redding is credited but relatively recent.
assessment.maturity: The foundational work is around 20 years old and well tested. Related quantitative work is still developing, so the discovery is mature but not fully settled in its welfare implications.
uncertainties: Missing credit for parallel contributors outside the credited list.
Prior trade-theory recognition (Krugman) may reduce committee appetite for the field.
Debate over how large the additional gains from selection are in quantitative models.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Mian and Sufi provided micro-data-based evidence that household leverage and credit supply drive housing booms, consumption collapses and unemployment in downturns. This changed how macroeconomists treat household balance sheets. It is a clear empirical advance with real relevance to crisis policy.
assessment.attribution: The contribution is a tight Mian–Sufi partnership, so attribution to the pair is clean. Campbell's broader household-finance work is substantial but distinct from this discovery.
assessment.maturity: The central papers date from 2009–2018. The results are widely cited and have been replicated across countries, though the work is younger than the other leading candidates. Debate about interpretation and about credit-supply versus demand explanations continues.
uncertainties: Relative recency compared with long-tested contributions.
Contested identification and the demand-versus-supply interpretation of the credit boom.
Overlap with other macro-finance work that the committee may prefer.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rubinstein's alternating-offers model gave bargaining theory a tractable non-cooperative foundation, and the Rubinstein–Wolinsky market bargaining model connected it to decentralised markets. These models are foundational for later work in matching, search and labour economics and bargaining applications across fields.
assessment.attribution: The alternating-offers result is clearly Rubinstein's, with Ståhl's related contribution outside the list. Wolinsky is the natural co-credit for bargaining in markets. Binmore contributed to the extensions and to the interpretation of the model, but his claim is less distinct.
assessment.maturity: The core results are from 1982–1985 and are among the most widely taught results in game theory. Time has fully confirmed their influence.
uncertainties: Whether a theory-only prize is competitive against more empirically influential candidates.
Credit boundary with Ståhl and Binmore.
Partial overlap with earlier recognition of game theory and market-institution design.
